--- title: "Week 09: Multiple Regression II" subtitle: "Date: October 22, 2026" footer: "[course-website](https://dharaden.github.io/psyc640/)" logo: "images/640_hex.png" format: revealjs: theme: [default, brand, clean.scss] multiplex: false transition: fade slide-number: true incremental: false chalkboard: true overview: false scrollable: true code-line-numbers: true editor: visual execute: echo: true freeze: auto editor_options: chunk_output_type: console --- ## Today... **Groups meet predictors.** - A group and a continuous predictor in the same model - Two lines, same slope: what "controlling for" looks like on a plot - What if the slope is **different** for each group? (interactions) - Simple slopes: the only honest way to report one - Why centering suddenly matters - An interaction that isn't there — and what to do about it ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(here) library(tidyverse) library(rio) library(broom) library(easystats) library(patchwork) options(scipen = 999) ``` ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Two threads, now braided ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} **Week 6** A group is a predictor. Dummy-code it, and the intercept is the reference group's mean. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Week 8** Put two predictors in one model and each coefficient becomes a *holding-constant* comparison. ::: ::::: . . . This week: a model with **both** kinds of predictor in it, and then the question neither week could ask — > Is the slope the same for every group? # Part 1: Group + Continuous ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## 20 students, two things we know about them 🎓 Daily study hours, final grade (on a 10-point scale), and whether the student worked with a **tutor**. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tutor <- import(here("files", "data", "tutor.csv")) %>% mutate(tutor_f = factor(tutor, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No tutor", "Tutor"))) tutor %>% group_by(tutor_f) %>% summarize(n = n(), study_m = mean(study), study_sd = sd(study), grade_m = mean(grade), grade_sd = sd(grade)) %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 6 tutor_f n study_m study_sd grade_m grade_sd 1 No tutor 10 0.995 0.563 6.76 1.14 2 Tutor 10 1.64 0.557 8.89 0.526 ``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Two separate stories ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_study <- lm(grade ~ study, data = tutor) m_tutor <- lm(grade ~ tutor_f, data = tutor) tidy(m_study) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 5 term estimate std.error statistic p.value 1 (Intercept) 5.52 0.450 12.3 3.46e-10 2 study 1.75 0.309 5.66 2.27e- 5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} tidy(m_tutor) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 5 term estimate std.error statistic p.value 1 (Intercept) 6.76 0.280 24.1 3.75e-15 2 tutor_fTutor 2.13 0.397 5.37 4.19e- 5 ``` ::: ::: ::: incremental - Study: each extra hour → **+1.75** grade points, $R^2$ = **.640** - Tutor: tutored students score **+2.13** higher, $R^2$ = **.616** ::: . . . Two strong, significant, nearly equally powerful predictors. Should we just add them up? ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Look first 👀 ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} tutor %>% ggplot(aes(x = study, y = grade, color = tutor_f)) + geom_point(size = 3, alpha = .85) + labs(x = "Daily study hours", y = "Final grade", color = NULL) + theme_bw(base_size = 16) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-09_interactions_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: . . . Notice where the tutored students **sit on the x-axis**. They also study more (1.64 vs 0.99 hours). The two predictors are entangled: *r* = **.52**. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Both at once ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_both <- lm(grade ~ study + tutor_f, data = tutor) summary(m_both) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = grade ~ study + tutor_f, data = tutor) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -0.8064 -0.4470 -0.2686 0.5413 0.9681 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 5.5882 0.3198 17.474 0.00000000000269 *** study 1.1777 0.2565 4.592 0.000259 *** tutor_fTutor 1.3751 0.3183 4.320 0.000465 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 0.6096 on 17 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.8285, Adjusted R-squared: 0.8083 F-statistic: 41.07 on 2 and 17 DF, p-value: 0.0000003096 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} glance(m_both) %>% select(r.squared, adj.r.squared, sigma) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 3 r.squared adj.r.squared sigma 1 0.829 0.808 0.610 ``` ::: ::: . . . | Predictor | Alone | Together | Change | |-----------|-------|-----------|--------| | `study` | 1.750 | **1.178** | −33% | | `tutor_f` | 2.130 | **1.375** | −35% | $R^2$: .640 → **.829** ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Both effects shrank. Both are still real. ::: incremental - Part of "the tutoring effect" was that tutored students **study more** - Part of "the studying effect" was that heavy studiers were **more likely to have a tutor** - Hold one still and each one keeps only the part that is *its own* ::: . . . ::: callout-important Shrinkage is not failure. The bivariate numbers were **double-counting** shared credit. These are the honest ones — and both survive: *p* = .0003 and *p* = .0005. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## What the model looks like $$\widehat{Grade} = 5.588 + 1.178(Study) + 1.375(Tutor)$$ ::: incremental - `Tutor` is 0 or 1, so this is **two lines** - No tutor: $\widehat{Grade} = 5.588 + 1.178(Study)$ - Tutor: $\widehat{Grade} = (5.588 + 1.375) +1.178(Study)$ ::: . . . Same slope. Different intercept. The model has **assumed** that tutoring shifts the line up without changing its steepness. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Parallel lines, by construction ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} tutor %>% mutate(fit = predict(m_both)) %>% ggplot(aes(x = study, y = grade, color = tutor_f)) + geom_point(size = 3, alpha = .6) + geom_line(aes(y = fit), linewidth = 1.2) + labs(x = "Daily study hours", y = "Final grade", color = NULL, title = "grade ~ study + tutor") + theme_bw(base_size = 16) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-09_interactions_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: The gap between the lines is **1.375 at every value of study**. That is not something we found. It is something we imposed. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Did the group earn its place? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} anova(m_study, m_both) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Model 1: grade ~ study Model 2: grade ~ study + tutor_f Res.Df RSS Df Sum of Sq F Pr(>F) 1 18 13.2498 2 17 6.3168 1 6.933 18.658 0.000465 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: incremental - $\Delta R^2$ = .829 − .640 = **.188** - $F$(1, 17) = **18.66**, *p* = .0005 - Typical miss: 0.858 → **0.610** grade points ::: . . . ::: callout-tip This is exactly the midterm's Part 6 table. One continuous predictor, one categorical predictor, one model with both, and the comparison between them. ::: # 💻 Your Turn - Part 1 [Open the activity](../class-activities/wk9_reproducibility.html){.button target="_blank"} # Part 2: What If The Slopes Differ? ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## The assumption we never checked Parallel lines say: *tutoring helps every student by the same amount, no matter how much they study.* . . . Is that plausible? ::: incremental - Maybe tutoring mostly helps students who are **not** putting in hours - Maybe tutoring compounds — it helps most the students who already study - Maybe it really is a constant boost ::: . . . We can **test** it. All it takes is one more term. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## The interaction term $$Y = b_0 + b_1X + b_2D + b_3(X \times D) + e$$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_int <- lm(grade ~ study * tutor_f, data = tutor) summary(m_int) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = grade ~ study * tutor_f, data = tutor) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -0.5728 -0.3837 -0.1584 0.1838 1.2555 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 5.0121 0.3496 14.337 0.00000000015 *** study 1.7567 0.3095 5.676 0.00003443132 *** tutor_fTutor 2.9203 0.6418 4.550 0.000328 *** study:tutor_fTutor -1.1713 0.4402 -2.661 0.017093 * --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 0.5232 on 16 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.8811, Adjusted R-squared: 0.8588 F-statistic: 39.53 on 3 and 16 DF, p-value: 0.0000001259 ``` ::: ::: . . . `study * tutor_f` in R expands to `study + tutor_f + study:tutor_f`. **Never** fit the product without both main effects. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## The interaction term ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sjPlot::tab_model(m_both, m_int) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
  grade grade
Predictors Estimates CI p Estimates CI p
(Intercept) 5.59 4.91 – 6.26 <0.001 5.01 4.27 – 5.75 <0.001
study 1.18 0.64 – 1.72 <0.001 1.76 1.10 – 2.41 <0.001
tutor f [Tutor] 1.38 0.70 – 2.05 <0.001 2.92 1.56 – 4.28 <0.001
study × tutor f [Tutor] -1.17 -2.10 – -0.24 0.017
Observations 20 20
R2 / R2 adjusted 0.829 / 0.808 0.881 / 0.859
````` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Reading the interaction | Term | *b* | *p* | What it is | |------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------| | intercept | $b_0$ 5.012 | \< .001 | grade for **no tutor**, study = 0 | | `study` | $b_1$ **1.757** | \< .001 | slope **for the reference group (no tutor)** | | `tutor_f` | $b_2$ 2.920 | .0003 | group gap **at study = 0 (intercept difference)** | | `study:tutor_f` | $b_3$ **−1.171** | **.017** | how much the slope **changes** for tutored students | . . . ::: callout-important Once there is an interaction in the model, `study` is **no longer "the" effect of studying.** It is the effect of studying *for the group coded 0*. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Simple slopes ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} **No tutor** $b_1 = 1.757$ Each extra hour → **+1.76** points ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Tutor** $b_1 + b_3 = 1.757 - 1.171$ Each extra hour → **+0.59** points ::: ::::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} coef(m_int)[["study"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1.756707 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} coef(m_int)[["study"]] + coef(m_int)[["study:tutor_fTutor"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.5853662 ``` ::: ::: . . . **Three times steeper** without a tutor. Report simple slopes — the raw coefficients mean almost nothing on their own. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Simple Slopes `modelbased` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} estimate_slopes(m_int, "study", by = "tutor_f") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimated Marginal Effects tutor_f | Slope | SE | 95% CI | t(16) | p -------------------------------------------------------- No tutor | 1.76 | 0.31 | [ 1.10, 2.41] | 5.68 | < .001 Tutor | 0.59 | 0.31 | [-0.08, 1.25] | 1.87 | 0.080 Marginal effects estimated for study Type of slope was dY/dX ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} plot(estimate_means(m_int, c("study", "tutor_f"))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-09_interactions_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Now the picture makes sense ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} tutor %>% ggplot(aes(x = study, y = grade, color = tutor_f)) + geom_point(size = 3, alpha = .6) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.2) + labs(x = "Daily study hours", y = "Final grade", color = NULL, title = "grade ~ study * tutor") + theme_bw(base_size = 16) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-09_interactions_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: The lines **converge**. Tutoring buys a lot for a student studying half an hour a day, and nearly nothing for one studying two hours. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Say it in words An interaction is always symmetric. Both of these are the same finding: ::: incremental - The **benefit of tutoring** depends on how much a student studies - The **payoff of studying** depends on whether a student has a tutor ::: . . . ::: callout-tip Pick the direction that answers your research question, say it in one sentence, then show the plot. A reader will believe the plot before they believe the coefficient. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Did the interaction earn its place? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} anova(m_both, m_int) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Model 1: grade ~ study + tutor_f Model 2: grade ~ study * tutor_f Res.Df RSS Df Sum of Sq F Pr(>F) 1 17 6.3168 2 16 4.3792 1 1.9376 7.0791 0.01709 * --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: | Model | $R^2$ | adj. $R^2$ | RSE | |----------------|-----------|------------|-----------| | additive | .8285 | .8083 | 0.610 | | \+ interaction | **.8811** | **.8588** | **0.523** | $\Delta R^2$ = **.053**, $F$(1, 16) = **7.08**, *p* = .017. Adjusted $R^2$ rose. Keep it. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## ⚠️ Centering is no longer optional {background-color="#FDF0D5"} In the interaction model, `tutor_f` = **2.92** was the group gap **at study = 0** — a student who studies zero hours a day. This doesn't exist. It is purely extrapolation. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tutor_c <- tutor %>% mutate(study_c = study - mean(study)) lm(grade ~ study_c * tutor_f, data = tutor_c) %>% tidy() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 5 term estimate std.error statistic p.value 1 (Intercept) 7.32 0.193 38.0 4.17e-17 2 study_c 1.76 0.310 5.68 3.44e- 5 3 tutor_fTutor 1.38 0.273 5.05 1.19e- 4 4 study_c:tutor_fTutor -1.17 0.440 -2.66 1.71e- 2 ``` ::: ::: ::: incremental - Mean `study` = **1.316** hours - Group gap at the **mean**: **1.379**, not 2.92 - `study_c` slope and the interaction: **identical** — centering did not change the model, only where we read it ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Why that matters ::: callout-important Centering a predictor moves the intercept and the **other** variable's main effect to a meaningful place. It does **not** change the interaction, the fit, or the *p*-value for the interaction. In a model with an interaction, always center your continuous predictor — or be ready to explain what X = 0 means. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-09_interactions_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: # Part 3: When It Isn't There ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## 100 children, sleep, and parenting 😴 Anxiety scores for 100 children, with hours of sleep and whether parenting was rated **Authoritative** or **Permissive**. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} kids <- import(here("files", "data", "child_wellbeing.csv")) %>% mutate(ps = factor(parenting_style, levels = c("Authoritative", "Permissive"))) kids %>% group_by(ps) %>% summarise(n = n(), sleep_m = mean(sleep_hours), anx_m = mean(anxiety_score), anx_sd = sd(anxiety_score)) %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 5 ps n sleep_m anx_m anx_sd 1 Authoritative 47 9.51 14.4 5.42 2 Permissive 53 9.36 30.0 6.46 ``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Build it up ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} k_sleep <- lm(anxiety_score ~ sleep_hours, data = kids) k_both <- lm(anxiety_score ~ sleep_hours + ps, data = kids) tidy(k_sleep) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 5 term estimate std.error statistic p.value 1 (Intercept) 67.8 7.79 8.70 8.17e-14 2 sleep_hours -4.78 0.822 -5.82 7.40e- 8 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} glance(k_sleep) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 12 r.squared adj.r.squared sigma statistic p.value df logLik AIC BIC 1 0.257 0.249 8.50 33.9 0.0000000740 1 -355. 716. 723. # ℹ 3 more variables: deviance , df.residual , nobs ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} tidy(k_both) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 5 term estimate std.error statistic p.value 1 (Intercept) 55.0 3.78 14.5 4.09e-26 2 sleep_hours -4.26 0.393 -10.9 1.92e-18 3 psPermissive 14.9 0.813 18.3 3.33e-33 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} glance(k_both) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 12 r.squared adj.r.squared sigma statistic p.value df logLik AIC BIC 1 0.833 0.830 4.05 242. 2.02e-38 2 -280. 568. 579. # ℹ 3 more variables: deviance , df.residual , nobs ``` ::: ::: ::: incremental - Sleep alone: **−4.78** per hour, $R^2$ = .257 - With parenting: **−4.26** per hour; permissive **+14.88**; $R^2$ = **.833** ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Note what did *not* happen The sleep slope moved from −4.78 to −4.26 — a **small** shrink. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} kids %>% group_by(ps) %>% summarise(mean_sleep = round(mean(sleep_hours), 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 2 ps mean_sleep 1 Authoritative 9.51 2 Permissive 9.36 ``` ::: ::: . . . The two groups sleep almost identically (9.51 vs 9.36 hours). With the predictors nearly unrelated, parenting had almost nothing to take back from sleep — it just explained a huge amount of **new** variance. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Test the interaction anyway ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} k_int <- lm(anxiety_score ~ sleep_hours * ps, data = kids) tidy(k_int) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 5 term estimate std.error statistic p.value 1 (Intercept) 52.9 6.17 8.57 1.71e-13 2 sleep_hours -4.04 0.645 -6.26 1.08e- 8 3 psPermissive 18.2 7.75 2.35 2.08e- 2 4 sleep_hours:psPermissive -0.353 0.815 -0.434 6.66e- 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} glance(k_int) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 12 r.squared adj.r.squared sigma statistic p.value df logLik AIC BIC 1 0.833 0.828 4.07 160. 3.24e-37 3 -280. 570. 583. # ℹ 3 more variables: deviance , df.residual , nobs ``` ::: ::: . . . `sleep_hours:psPermissive` = **−0.353**, *p* = **.666**. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## The fit table tells the story | Model | $R^2$ | adj. $R^2$ | RSE | |----------------|-------|--------------|-----------| | additive | .8330 | **.8295** | **4.048** | | \+ interaction | .8333 | **.8281** ⬇️ | 4.066 ⬆️ | ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} anova(k_both, k_int) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Model 1: anxiety_score ~ sleep_hours + ps Model 2: anxiety_score ~ sleep_hours * ps Res.Df RSS Df Sum of Sq F Pr(>F) 1 97 1589.8 2 96 1586.7 1 3.1077 0.188 0.6655 ``` ::: ::: $\Delta R^2$ = **.0003**, $F$(1, 96) = **0.19**, *p* = .666. Adjusted $R^2$ went **down**. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Parallel lines — this time earned ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} kids %>% ggplot(aes(x = sleep_hours, y = anxiety_score, color = ps)) + geom_point(alpha = .6) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.2) + labs(x = "Sleep (hours)", y = "Anxiety score", color = NULL) + theme_bw(base_size = 16) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-09_interactions_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: Two lines, essentially the same slope, clearly different heights. **Sleep matters the same amount in both groups; the groups just start in different places.** ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## The discipline ::: incremental 1. **Fit** the interaction if you have a reason to expect one 2. **Test** it 3. If it is not there, **report that** and interpret the additive model 4. Do **not** keep an interaction you cannot defend just because it was your idea ::: . . . ::: callout-warning A non-significant interaction is **not** evidence that the slopes are identical — especially with small groups, where you have very little power to detect a difference in slopes. "We found no evidence of moderation" ≠ "there is no moderation." ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## The write-up: interaction present > Final grade was regressed on daily study hours (centered), tutoring status, and their interaction (*N* = 20). The full model accounted for 88.1% of the variance in grades, *F*(3, 16) = 39.53, *p* \< .001. The interaction was significant, *b* = −1.17, *SE* = 0.44, *t*(16) = −2.66, *p* = .017, Δ*R²* = .053. Simple slopes indicated that each additional hour of daily study was associated with a 1.76-point increase in grade for students without a tutor, but only a 0.59-point increase for students with a tutor. At the mean level of study, tutored students scored 1.38 points higher than untutored students (*p* \< .001). ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## The write-up: interaction absent > Anxiety was regressed on hours of sleep and parenting style (*N* = 100). The additive model accounted for 83.3% of the variance, *F*(2, 97) = 241.87, *p* \< .001. Each additional hour of sleep was associated with a 4.26-point decrease in anxiety, holding parenting style constant (*p* \< .001), and children with permissive parenting scored 14.88 points higher than those with authoritative parenting, holding sleep constant (*p* \< .001). A sleep × parenting interaction was tested and was not supported, *b* = −0.35, *p* = .666, Δ*R²* = .0003; the additive model is therefore reported. . . . ::: callout-tip Report that you **tested** it. A reader who cannot tell whether you looked will assume you looked and did not like the answer. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## For next time ::: callout-important ## 📂 Midterm Project — due **Tuesday 10/27 at 11:59pm** Five days. If Part 6 is not drafted by this weekend, it will not be good by Tuesday. You are **not** required to include an interaction. If you fit one, test it and report the test either way. ::: 📖 Chapter 11 — ROS · Chapter 12.1 — ST (assumptions and diagnostics) **Next week:** everything we have been glancing at on residual plots becomes a named assumption with an actual test.

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
